content: Any labels or markings indicating the presence of an infectious substance must be removed or obliterated. Packing Instruction P650 applies to UN 3373 Category A substances. Packaging must be of high quality and durable enough to withstand the typical shocks and loads encountered during transport, including trans-shipment between cargo units, warehouses, and manual or mechanical handling. The packaging must consist of three components: 1. A primary receptacle. 2. A secondary packaging. 3. An outer packaging, with either the secondary or outer packaging being rigid. Primary receptacles must be packed within secondary packaging in a manner that prevents breakage, puncture, or leakage under normal transport conditions. Secondary packaging must be secured within the outer packaging using appropriate cushioning material. Any leakage must not compromise the integrity of the cushioning material or the outer packaging. For transport, the outer packaging must display a diamond-shaped mark with a minimum side length of 50 mm, a line width of at least 2 mm, and letters/numbers at least 6 mm high. The mark must be on a contrasting background, clearly visible, and legible. The proper shipping name, BIOLOGICAL SUBSTANCE, CATEGORY B, must also be marked adjacent to the diamond-shaped mark in letters at least 6 mm high. The outer packaging must have at least one surface with minimum dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm. The packaging must withstand a 2-meter drop in any orientation without leakage from the primary receptacle(s), which must remain protected by absorbent material (if required) within the secondary packaging. This capability can be demonstrated through testing, assessment, or experience. For liquid substances: 1. The primary receptacle(s) must be leakproof. 2. The secondary packaging must be leakproof. 3. If multiple fragile primary receptacles are used in a single secondary packaging, they must be individually wrapped or separated to prevent contact. 4. Absorbent material must be placed between the primary receptacle(s) and the secondary packaging. For solid substances: 1. The primary receptacle(s) must be siftproof. 2. The secondary packaging must be siftproof. 3. If multiple fragile primary receptacles are used in a single secondary packaging, they must be individually wrapped or separated to prevent contact. 4. If there is any doubt about residual liquid presence in the primary receptacle, packaging suitable for liquids, including absorbent materials, must be used. When ice is used for transport, it must be placed outside the secondary packaging or within the outer packaging or overpack. Interior supports must secure the secondary packaging in its original position. The outer packaging or overpack must be leakproof, and the primary and secondary packaging must maintain their integrity at the temperature of the refrigerant used, as well as under conditions of refrigeration loss. If packages are placed in an overpack, the required package markings must either be visible or reproduced on the outside of the overpack. Infectious substances assigned to UN 3373 that are packed and marked according to this instruction are not subject to additional requirements in these regulations. Small quantities of dangerous goods (30 mL or less) from Classes 3 (flammable liquids), 8 (corrosives), or 9 (miscellaneous dangerous substances) may be included in each primary receptacle containing infectious substances, provided they are packed in accordance with this instruction. Packing Instruction P621 applies to UN 3291. Packaging must include sufficient absorbent material to retain all liquid present and must conform to Packing Group II performance levels for solids. For larger quantities of liquid, drums, jerricans, or composite packaging must meet Packing Group II performance levels for liquids. Packing Instruction PI954 applies to UN 1845 (Carbon dioxide, solid or Dry ice) for passenger and cargo aircraft. Dangerous goods transport documentation is not required if alternative written documentation describing the contents is provided. The net mass of dry ice must be marked on the outside of the package. When dry ice is shipped in a unit load device prepared by a single shipper, prior arrangements must be made with the operator. The unit load device must not contain dangerous goods other than UN 3373 (Biological substance, Category B) or ID 8000 (Consumer commodity). The shipper must provide the operator with written documentation or electronic data stating the total quantity of dry ice in the unit load device. Export Regulations: If exporting infectious substances potentially covered by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), an export permit must be obtained from the relevant governmental authority. This typically involves proving the material was legally obtained and that its export will not harm the species' survival. Both exporting and importing countries usually need to issue permits for CITES-listed materials. If the material falls under the Nagoya Protocol or Access and Benefit-sharing (ABS) legislation, compliance with domestic and international regulations is required. This may involve obtaining prior informed consent and negotiating a Material Transfer Agreement (MTA) to outline benefit-sharing terms. Import Regulations: When importing infectious substances, compliance with biosafety and biosecurity regulations is essential. Dual-use substances may require a risk assessment and adherence to strict security protocols. If the material is CITES-regulated, permits and certificates must be obtained, and packaging must meet stringent requirements. For materials under the Nagoya Protocol, prior informed consent and an MTA may be necessary. Documentation and compliance with ABS provisions are critical to avoid penalties. The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety regulates the transboundary movement of living modified organisms (LMOs), including GMOs. Importing GMOs requires an Advanced Informed Agreement (AIA) with the exporting country, a risk assessment, and approval from the importing nation's competent authority. Registration and Notification: In some jurisdictions, importing infectious substances requires registration or notification, particularly for materials classified under UN 2814, UN 2900, or UN 3373. Basel Convention: The importing country must confirm its ability to manage infectious waste and validate its receipt upon arrival. The waste must be treated or disposed of in an environmentally sound manner, with precise records maintained as mandated by the Basel Convention.
